summary.summary: Covering report presenting the draft Annual Governance Statement for 2025/26 (the AGS itself is Appendix 1, a separate document). Two points matter for a lender. First, the draft AGS has been published alongside the council's draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, with the final versions due by the 31 January 2027 statutory deadline after a further update in October 2026 — the reporting cycle is on its statutory track. Second, the council says no NEW significant governance issues have arisen since the final 2024/25 AGS was approved in February 2026, but the existing ones continue: the draft focuses on updating progress on financial sustainability, improvement and transformation, governance and internal control, leadership capacity, children's services improvement and partnership working. In short, a council still working through a known list of significant issues, with no fresh deterioration disclosed and no figures in this paper.

signals.headline: Draft AGS 2025/26 published alongside the draft 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, in line with statutory requirements; final accountability statements due by the 31 January 2027 backstop after an October 2026 committee update
signals.why: The unaudited 2025/26 balance sheet is now public and the governance disclosures around it are on the statutory timetable rather than slipping.

compliance.notes: High-quality, Arlingclose-advised strategy: strongest areas are the liability benchmark (charted to the end of the debt profile with all balances and assumptions), the full prudential-indicator suite, the capital strategy/MRP and a comprehensive investment strategy covering the council's ~£60m of service/commercial investments. Weakest areas are formal governance artefacts not restated in the annual documents (no explicit adoption of the TM Code's four clauses; no audit-qualification flag; no explicit sterling-only borrowing statement or paras 51-53 compliance statement; no formal IMPs), and, for a commercial investor, no quantified commercial/service-income dependence ratio. Note: the packet's capital_strategy.url (s134122) was a 2027/28 MTFS-assumptions Cabinet paper with no capital-strategy content; the real Capital/Investment strategies and prudential indicators were read from the MTFS 2026-2030 full report (Annexes 5, 6, B, C). The packet TMSS url (s131504) was a cover report; the real TMSS is Annex 7 (s131505).

Annex 6 paras 6.46-6.47 (Prudential Code changes / government opposition to commercial property referenced), 6.69 (guidance followed)

news_drafts.headline: Cheshire East finds £4.652m of savings, cutting its 2027/28 budget gap from £15.271m to £10.619m
news_drafts.lead:
Cheshire East Council has identified £4.652m of savings towards its 2027/28 budget, reducing the gap in its plans from £15.271m to £10.619m, according to a report to Cabinet on 8 October. The savings came from three joint workshops between the Corporate Leadership Team and Cabinet. The remaining gap still depends on exceptional financial support (EFS), government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending, which is a last resort. The council also used it for 2026/27.

The report's medium-term financial strategy (MTFS), the council's financial plan for the next few years, puts the gap at £14.137m in 2028/29 and £19.827m in 2029/30. It falls to £6.890m in 2030/31 as planned rebuilding of reserves begins, which assumes future savings are delivered. The allowance for pay inflation rises from £16.427m in 2026/27 to £38.503m in 2030/31. The paper says reliance on EFS "is not sustainable in the medium to long term". It also says usable reserves, the part of its reserves the council can spend, remain "materially below the risk-assessed level".

The first-quarter performance report shows revenue budget monitoring, the in-year check of spending against budget, in an underspend at the end of the quarter, though no amount is given. It forecasts a shortfall in transformation savings, mainly in Children's Services, with alternatives being explored. Asset disposal is "significantly below target" after a major sale at Earl Road was delayed. Vacancies and agency use rose, and sickness absence worsened.

Cabinet also has a revised Council Tax Support scheme, which reduces bills for low-income households. Modelling puts its cost at £20.024m against £22.150m now, a £2.126m difference, with 306 working-age households (2.8%) losing all support. The section 151 officer, the council's chief finance officer, says this is not automatically a cashable saving.

news_drafts.headline: Cheshire East balanced its 2026/27 budget using £24.995m of government-approved emergency borrowing permission
news_drafts.lead:
Cheshire East Council balanced its 2026/27 budget by using exceptional financial support, with a capitalisation direction totalling £24.995m, according to a quarter one forecast outturn report before its Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 7 October. Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. A capitalisation direction is government permission to treat day-to-day spending as if it were capital spending, so it can be paid for by borrowing or asset sales.

The council set the budget in February 2026. The report says: "The budget was balanced, as required by statute, with planned use of EFS, by way of a capitalisation direction, totalling £24.995m." The support was planned from the outset, not added during the year to cover an overspend.

The report says the use of this support forms part of the council's medium-term financial strategy, its financial plan for the following years, which runs through to 2030. The papers verified for this item do not give the amount in later years, or the forecast position for the year at quarter one.

news_drafts.headline: Cheshire East balanced its 2026/27 budget using £24.995m of government-approved exceptional financial support
news_drafts.lead:
Cheshire East Council balanced its 2026/27 budget by planning to use £24.995m of exceptional financial support (EFS), according to the first-quarter forecast report put to its Adults Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 24 September. EFS is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort.

The support comes through a capitalisation direction, which is government permission to treat day-to-day spending as if it were capital spending, meaning money spent on things that last, so it can be paid for by borrowing or asset sales. The report says the budget "was balanced, as required by statute, with planned use of EFS, by way of a capitalisation direction, totalling £24.995m". The figure was part of the budget as set, not a change made during the year.

The council operates under the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023, which amended section 12A of the Local Government Act 2003 to give government powers over councils' capital finance risk, including provision for directions to reduce that risk. The papers supplied for this report give no breakdown of which services the £24.995m covers, and no forecast for the year's final position.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2027/28 and MTFS 2027/31 UpdateCabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Council operating under external scrutiny: CIPFA Assurance Review (May 2026, published August 2026) and extended non-statutory Best Value Notice (issued July 2026).
findings.detail: CIPFA Assurance Review completed and published in 2026. Extended non-statutory Best Value Notice issued July 2026. Council developing Sustainability Strategy in response. These external assessments provide regulatory context for urgency of financial recovery.
findings.matters: External professional and regulatory scrutiny of council governance and performance indicates systemic concerns; affects council's credibility, capacity to borrow, and authority to make changes.
findings.figures: Review completion/publication May-August 2026; Notice issued July 2026
findings.quote: in line with the CIPFA Assurance Review of May 2026, published in August 2026, and the extended non-statutory Best Value Notice, notified to the Council in July 2026

findings.paper_title: Budget 2027/28 and MTFS 2027/31 UpdateCabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Pay inflation assumptions more than double over four-year MTFS period, from £16.427m to £38.503m.
findings.detail: Pay inflation grows from £16.427m in 2026/27 to £38.503m in 2030/31, an increase of £22.076m. This is a major structural cost pressure driven by employment market factors largely outside council control and grows faster than other central budget lines.
findings.matters: Pay awards are an uncontrollable cost driver; this doubling represents a major structural pressure accounting for significant share of growing deficits across the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2027/28 and MTFS 2027/31 UpdateCabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Usable reserves materially below risk-assessed level, limiting shock absorption capacity.
findings.detail: Council explicitly states reserves are inadequate. Demand pressures, uncertain savings delivery, and balance-sheet risks combine to leave limited financial flexibility. Future years include planned reserve top-ups but baseline position remains below requirement.
findings.matters: Low reserves remove the buffer to absorb cost pressures, savings delivery failures, or unexpected financial shocks without corrective action.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures disclosed; Table 2 shows planned reserve top-ups in later years but current levels unstated
findings.quote: Usable reserves remain materially below the risk-assessed level, and demand-led pressures, savings delivery and wider balance-sheet risks leave limited capacity to absorb further financial shocks without corrective action or changes to the recovery plan.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2027/28 and MTFS 2027/31 UpdateCabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Council's financial position requires continued Exceptional Financial Support, described as "not sustainable in the medium to long term
findings.detail: Council used Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 and continues to require it for future years. Paper explicitly states this is not sustainable in the medium to long term and requires urgent action. EFS is temporary emergency measure, not a financial solution.
findings.matters: Continued emergency funding dependency indicates systemic structural deficit rather than cyclical pressure, with escalating funding risk if the situation worsens.
findings.figures: EFS required each year; Table 2 shows funding shortfalls after normal revenue sources exhausted
findings.quote: This is not sustainable in the medium to long term and needs to be addressed urgently for the Council to be financially sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Budget 2027/28 and MTFS 2027/31 UpdateCabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Four-year deficits worsen from £10.619m in 2027/28 to peak of £19.827m in 2029/30, then improve to £6.890m in 2030/31.
findings.detail: Despite 2027/28 savings, the medium-term outlook shows deficits growing in years two and three, with 2029/30 the worst year. Deficits reduce in 2030/31 as planned reserve rebuilding begins, but this assumes all future savings are delivered as planned.
findings.matters: The largest deficit year is not the immediate budget but 2029/30, indicating structural pressures that are getting worse before improving, and dependency on sustained future savings delivery.
findings.quote: This level of saving has improved the financial position of each year of the MTFS and is represented in table 2 overleaf.

daily_post.headline: The Adult Social Care transformation designed to address structural budget pressures remains in pre-design phase, with implementation deferred to 2027.
daily_post.lead: The council's ability to close structural annual gaps (£2-3m) depends on transformation outcomes. A lender needs to understand timeline risk: delays in design or implementation would extend the period of structural budget pressure.
